title: Open-Ended and Closed-Ended Questions

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a question as a container you hand someone to fill. A closed-ended question is a small cup: only a drop fits, such as 'yes,' 'no,' or a number. An open-ended question is an empty bowl: the person decides how much to pour in and in what order. 'Tell me about your day' is a bowl; 'Was your day good?' is a cup. Same topic, very different amount of information comes back, and the difference was built into the question before the person ever spoke.

### Question 2

The first word of a question is usually a strong clue. Stems such as 'Do,' 'Did,' 'Have,' 'Is,' and 'Are' set up a two-way door: yes or no. Stems such as 'What,' 'How,' and 'Tell me about' open a hallway the person can walk down as far as they choose. Here, 'Have you taken...' is a two-way door. Treat this as a reliable rule of thumb rather than a law, because a 'what' question can still be closed if the answer set is tiny, as in 'What is your date of birth?'

### Question 3

Compare filling out a form with writing a story. Closed-ended questions are the form: name, dose, how many times a day, yes or no. They produce exact entries quickly and are easy to check. Open-ended questions are the story: they tell you what the experience was like and what the patient thinks matters. Both are useful, but when a specific fact has to be right and recorded, the form is the tool you reach for.

### Question 4

Picture two light sources. An open-ended question is a lantern: it lights the whole room, so you notice things you did not know were there. A closed-ended question is a laser pointer: it lights one exact spot brilliantly and everything else stays dark. The laser is more precise about that spot, but it can only point where you already decided to aim. Skilled interviewers use the lantern first to find what matters, then the laser to pin down the details.

### Question 5

Imagine fishing with a net whose only opening is shaped like a goldfish. You will catch goldfish and nothing else, no matter what else is in the water, and you will walk away convinced the lake holds only goldfish. Yes/no questions work the same way: the answers can only be shaped like the guesses you brought with you. What is missing never announces itself, which is exactly what makes this pattern hard to notice from the inside.

### Question 6

Compare 'Do you like broccoli?' with 'You don't like broccoli, right?' The second version has already told you which answer the asker expects, and disagreeing now means correcting them, so many people simply go along. That is what makes it leading. The problem is not that the question is answerable with one word; it is that the answer was supplied before the person opened their mouth. Strip out the expectation and the same closed question becomes usable.

### Question 7

Rebuilding a question often takes only the first word. Open with 'Are,' 'Do,' or 'Is' and you have constructed a yes/no box before the topic even appears. Open with 'What,' 'How,' or 'Tell me about' and the box is gone. The test is not the wording itself but the answer set: ask whether the question already contains the list of acceptable replies. 'What is your age?' begins with 'what' yet still has one narrow answer, so check the answer set rather than trusting the first word alone.

### Question 8

Consider how a drawing is built: the large shapes come first and the fine detail comes last, because detail added to a wrong outline is wasted effort. Opening wide is the outline, and it shows you what the patient's problem actually looks like from the inside. The closed follow-ups are the detail that makes the record accurate and usable. Reversing the order, or skipping either stage, leaves you with a picture that is either precise about the wrong thing or vague about everything.

### Question 9

An open-ended question is like being handed a blank page and told to write a paragraph. For many people that freedom is welcome; for someone whose memory and word-finding are failing, the blank page is exhausting and can feel like a test they are failing in public. A closed question is closer to a two-item menu they can point at. Shrinking the task is not condescension, it is offering a version of the question the person can actually complete.

### Question 10

Imagine a server who asks, 'Pizza, pasta, or soup?' when what you actually wanted was a sandwich. Most people do not argue with the menu; they pick pasta and eat something they did not want. The menu was written before you spoke, so anything absent from it quietly disappears and never shows up in the record of what you ordered. Asking 'What are you in the mood for?' costs one extra sentence and leaves room for the sandwich.

### Question 11

'How are you?' exchanged in a hallway is not really a question, it is a greeting with words in it, and 'fine' is the greeting returned. The grammar is wide open, but the script is so familiar that both people run it automatically. Breaking the script requires aiming the question at something specific and recent: 'What has your breathing been like this week?' The aim signals that you are asking for real information, which gives the other person permission to stop reciting.

### Question 12

Asking a friend to describe their week gives you a vivid account and probably a surprise or two, but it will not tell you what time they took each pill. Some tasks are inventories, and an inventory needs inventory questions: which drug, what strength, how many times a day, when was the last dose. Open questions are what surface the item nobody asked about, such as a supplement the patient never counted as medicine. Closed questions are what guarantee no required field is left blank. Drop either one and the reconciliation has a hole in it.
